In 1913 income per head in Latvia and Estonia stood at the level of Finland or Italy, and even agrarian Lithuania was richer than Greece or Portugal \parencite[129--30]{norkus_2023_output}. When Red Army soldiers entered the Baltic republics under the mutual-assistance pacts of 1939 they wrote home in astonishment: `the store is full of all sorts of fabrics, whatever the soul desires, and there is not a single person, not to mention a line' \parencite[279]{meltyukhov2014en}. By 1990, after forty-five years inside the Soviet Union, income per head in the three republics was about half that of Finland and three-fifths that of the Western periphery; by 2024, after three decades of reform, European Union membership and `Baltic tiger' growth, they remained in Europe's periphery, and the richest of them in 1913, Latvia, had become the poorest \parencite[93]{koll_2025_reinterpretation}. Three small, literate, egalitarian economies, which possessed from the outset much of what the catch-up literature regards as the social capability needed to grow \parencite[388]{abramovitz1986}, have failed over 110 years and under three economic regimes to leave the periphery into which the nineteenth century placed them. The gap has begun to close.
